title: Pakistan's Fuel Crisis Deepens as IMF-Driven Price Hikes Spark Transport Strike Threats
excerpt: Daily fuel price revisions, soaring diesel costs, and Middle East supply disruptions have pushed Pakistan's transport sector to the brink of a nationwide shutdown.
body:
• Pakistan switched to daily fuel price revisions on July 21 under IMF conditionalities, triggering protests from transporters and petroleum dealers
  • Diesel prices surged by PKR 31 per litre in a single revision, with diesel now at PKR 354 per litre and petrol at PKR 316 per litre
  • The Pakistan Goods Transport Alliance has warned that a nationwide strike call could come "at any time," threatening supply chains for food, fuel, and medicines
  • Petroleum dealers are demanding margins be raised from 2.68% to 8% and have scheduled an emergency meeting for August 10
  • Pakistan is scrambling to secure alternative crude oil supplies from the US, Nigeria, and Singapore as Middle East routes face disruption

Pakistan's transport and fuel sectors are on a collision course with the federal government as IMF-mandated fuel price reforms and the Middle East crisis combine to create what industry leaders are calling an existential threat to their businesses.

"Transporters across Pakistan should remain prepared; a nationwide strike call can be given at any time," Malik Shehzad Awan, president of the Pakistan Goods Transport Alliance, warned in a statement on Friday, branding the government's new daily pricing mechanism as "anti-transport policies."

The Daily Pricing Gamble

At the heart of the crisis is Pakistan's decision to begin revising gasoline and diesel prices on a daily basis, effective July 21. The move, which the government says brings transparency by reflecting international oil market movements in real time, was a key condition set by the International Monetary Fund as part of Pakistan's ongoing bailout programme.

The immediate impact has been devastating for the transport sector. In a single revision, diesel prices jumped by PKR 31.05 per litre, pushing the cost to PKR 354.35 per litre. Petrol rose by PKR 5.44 to PKR 316.15 per litre. For an industry already operating on razor-thin margins, the volatility has made business planning nearly impossible.

"Many road freight businesses face closure due to the frequent hikes of diesel prices."

— Malik Shehzad Awan, President, Pakistan Goods Transport Alliance

Transport Sector at Breaking Point

The Karachi Goods Carriers Association has gone further, rejecting the price hikes outright and warning of a nationwide wheel-jam strike if the decision is not withdrawn. General Secretary Nadeem Akhtar Arain said transporters would stop all movement of goods, close offices, and launch coordinated protests across the country.

The implications of such a shutdown would be severe. Pakistan's road freight network carries the bulk of the country's imports and exports through ports in Karachi, Port Qasim, and Gwadar. A strike would disrupt the distribution of fuel, food, and medicines — commodities that Pakistan can ill afford to have in short supply.

Petroleum dealers have their own grievances. The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association has demanded that dealer margins be raised from the current 2.68% to 8%, arguing that current profits of roughly PKR 8 per litre are unsustainable. An emergency meeting has been scheduled for August 10 to finalise a protest strategy.

Middle East Supply Crunch

Compounding the domestic crisis is the escalating Middle East conflict, which threatens Pakistan's oil supply lines. Pakistan relies heavily on crude imports transiting the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, both of which face heightened security risks.

In response, Pakistani refiners have begun exploring alternative crude oil sources from the United States, Nigeria, Singapore, and Central Asia. Federal Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik briefed industry representatives on the supply threats earlier this week, prompting an urgent diversification push.

"The transport sector is the backbone of the economy. Repeated fuel price increases have pushed operators into a severe financial crisis."

— Nadeem Akhtar Arain, General Secretary, Karachi Goods Carriers Association

The IMF Tightrope

Pakistan's predicament is a familiar one. The country is in its latest IMF programme, which requires subsidy removal and energy price reforms in exchange for continued disbursements. Previous governments have faced similar pressure — Islamabad has now secured 13 IMF bailouts since the late 1980s — but the current confluence of external supply shocks and domestic political instability makes this iteration particularly volatile.

The government has attempted to defuse tensions, with Minister Malik meeting petroleum dealers and offering assurances that margins would be reviewed within two weeks. A trial period for the daily pricing mechanism has been proposed, with results to be evaluated in consultation with stakeholders.

What's Next

All eyes are on the August 10 emergency meeting of petroleum dealers, which could determine whether Pakistan faces a coordinated fuel supply disruption. The Pakistan Goods Transport Alliance has left its strike date open-ended, adding to the uncertainty. For ordinary Pakistanis already grappling with inflation and currency depreciation, the prospect of fuel shortages and supply chain breakdowns represents yet another economic blow.
